pr.title: Accelerate GVN a little
pr.description:
This PR addresses a few inefficiencies I've seen in callgrind profiles.

Commits are independent.

Only the first commit introduces a change in behaviour: we stop substituting some constant pointers. But we keep propagating their contents that have no provenance, so we don't lose much.

pr.author: cjgillot

processing.reason: No source-grounded counterexample is valid here. The PR's behavioral change stops GVN from propagating a pointer-valued scalar constant and instead leaves the value flowing through the originating local (e.g. `_3 = _9; _2 = _9 as &[u32]`). But in MIR/const-eval semantics, `_9` and the propagated `const {ALLOC0<imm>: &[u32; 3]}` designate the same promoted allocation at the same offset; likewise `_9` and `const {ALLOC1<imm>: &std::alloc::Global}` designate the same ZST allocation. Thus a faithful pair (local copy vs. const-pointer substitution) passes Miri and produces identical numeric/boolean/address results. The PR's stated hazard is that such pointers “may lose part of their identity in codegen” (FIXME #79738), not an interpreter-visible value change. To force a difference in Miri I would have to fabricate distinct allocations for the constant mentions, strip/invent provenance, or otherwise encode a different rewrite; that would not be the historical GVN transformation and could also make one side fail Miri. So there is no legitimate original/incorrect pair with identical inputs that both pass Miri and yield different defined results.

analysis.originalLogic: GVN's constant propagation helper `op_to_prop_const` recognized a constant with scalar ABI, read it via the interpreter, and returned `Some(ConstValue::Scalar(scalar))` whenever `ecx.read_scalar(op)` succeeded and `scalar.try_to_scalar_int().is_ok()`. Thus scalar pointers, for which `try_to_scalar_int` fails, were also turned into `ConstValue::Scalar` and could be propagated into MIR operands by GVN. Additional original bookkeeping: `next_opaque` started at 0, `try_as_constant` checked `value.is_deterministic()` to decide whether a `Value::Constant` was safe to mention again, `simplify_operand` normalized constant operands before `insert_constant`, `simplify_place_projection` used `place.is_indirect()`, and `rev_locals`/`values`/`evaluated` were created without capacity estimates and `rev_locals` was grown via `ensure_contains_elem`.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historically incorrect transformation was: when GVN's `op_to_prop_const` successfully reads a scalar-ABI constant whose scalar is a pointer rather than an integer, it returns `Some(ConstValue::Scalar(scalar))`, allowing GVN to substitute that constant pointer directly into MIR. The PR describes this as stopping substitution of some constant pointers because those pointers may lose part of their identity in codegen (FIXME rust-lang/rust#79738). The corrected code instead does `if !scalar.try_to_scalar_int().is_ok() { ... return None; }`, so non-integer/pointer scalars are not returned as `ConstValue::Scalar`. The test diffs show the effect: an operand that had become a pointer constant such as `_4 = const {ALLOC0<imm>: &[u32; 3]};` or `_2 = const {ALLOC0<imm>: &[u32; 3]} as &[u32] (PointerCoercion(Unsize));` is instead left referring to the prior local: `_3 = _9; _2 = _9 as &[u32] (PointerCoercion(Unsize));`. Similarly `_6 = ...alloc_impl(const {ALLOC1<imm>: &std::alloc::Global}, ...)` becomes `_6 = ...alloc_impl(_9, ...)`. This is not merely the fixed implementation: the wrong rewrite is to propagate any readable scalar constant, including pointer-valued constants, as a `ConstValue::Scalar`; the safe condition is to restrict that path to scalar integers.
analysis.inputDomain: MIR bodies processed by the GVN MIR optimization pass that contain constants/operands with pointer-valued scalar ABI, especially promoted references, slices, references to zero-sized types, and constants used as call operands. The supplied regressions exercise `(&[1u32, 2, 3] as &[u32])[1]` in `tests/mir-opt/const_prop/slice_len.rs` and the `issue_117368_print_invalid_constant` pre-codegen test involving `&std::alloc::Global` and a `Layout` constant. The relevant input condition is a constant with `Abi::Scalar(abi::Scalar::Initialized { .. })` whose read scalar is not convertible to `ScalarInt` (a pointer), as opposed to ordinary integer/bool scalars that remain valid to propagate.
analysis.summary: GVN PR "Accelerate GVN a little" includes one behavioral change plus performance/capacity changes. The reusable correctness knowledge is that GVN must not propagate pointer-valued constants through `op_to_prop_const`; it now returns `None` for non-integer scalars to avoid leaking pointers whose identity may be lost in codegen. The other commits preallocate GVN containers, lazily grow `rev_locals`, use `disambiguator == 0` for deterministic constants with `next_opaque` starting at 1, and switch projection simplification to `is_indirect_first_projection`. Regression MIR tests show pointer constants are no longer substituted while integer scalar propagation is retained.
analysis.trigger: During GVN simplification, `op_to_prop_const` reads a scalar-ABI constant and `read_scalar` yields a scalar for which `try_to_scalar_int()` is not `Ok` (a pointer), then GVN would previously convert it to `ConstValue::Scalar` and substitute it into an operand/place. This is triggered by MIR involving promoted references/slices or references to ZSTs, such as `&[1u32, 2, 3] as &[u32]` and `&std::alloc::Global`, when the GVN MIR test harness runs.
preconditions: The GVN MIR optimization pass is running on the body.
A constant operand has scalar ABI matching `Abi::Scalar(abi::Scalar::Initialized { .. })`.
The read scalar is a pointer, i.e. `scalar.try_to_scalar_int()` fails rather than returning `Ok`.
The constant value flows through GVN's constant insertion/simplification so it can be replaced by a `ConstValue::Scalar`.
pitfalls: Do not treat the whole PR as only a performance change: the first commit deliberately stops substituting some constant pointers and is the behavioral part.

Do not conflate the pointer-suppression change in `op_to_prop_const` with the separate `disambiguator`/determinism refactor (`disambiguator: 0` means deterministic, `next_opaque: Some(1)`) or with `is_indirect_first_projection` replacing `is_indirect`.
Do not claim the preallocation changes (`with_capacity`, lazy `rev_locals`) alter semantics; the PR describes them as reducing allocations and amortizing allocations.
Do not assume all scalar constants are safe to propagate; integer scalar constants remain propagatable, but pointer scalars must return `None`.
Do not infer from a retained test name or old comment that a replacement pass is wrong; compare the actual MIR assignments in the decoded revisions.
No compiler was built or executed for this analysis; do not claim reproduction or runtime confirmation.
analysis.testStrategy: Use the existing MIR regression dumps under `tests/mir-opt/const_prop/slice_len.main.GVN.*.diff` and `tests/mir-opt/pre-codegen/issue_117368_print_invalid_constant.main.GVN.*.diff`. Compare two GVN runs that differ only in whether `op_to_prop_const` returns pointer scalars: with the incorrect transformation, expect pointer constants such as `const {ALLOC0<imm>: &[u32; 3]}` or `const {ALLOC1<imm>: &std::alloc::Global}` to be substituted into operands (and extra ALLOC dumps); with the correct behavior, expect references to remain via the source local (`_3 = _9; _2 = _9 as &[u32] (PointerCoercion(Unsize));`, `_6 = ...alloc_impl(_9, ...)`) and no leaked pointer constant. Also check `tests/mir-opt/const_prop/slice_len.rs`, where the CHECK line changed from requiring a constant slice to allowing the prior local, and `tests/incremental/hashes/for_loops.rs`, where `optimized_mir` is no longer expected to differ for `cfail2`/`cfail5`. Include a control case with ordinary integer scalar constants to confirm they still propagate.
evidence: Only the first commit introduces a change in behaviour: we stop substituting some constant pointers. But we keep propagating their contents that have no provenance, so we don't lose much.
